title: Painted beams
hook: he had favorite sayings from the Bible and the classics painted on his library beams

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tower: Montaigne climbing to his round library to write tries, essais, about himself. Your line was my tower. Where did you find ten minutes of your own? Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

A sticky note on a bathroom mirror. A line of a poem taped above a kitchen sink. Somebody's grandmother's handwriting on an index card, stuck to the fridge with a magnet shaped like a lemon. People put words where their eyes will land when they're not trying to read. Montaigne did it too, but with paint, and overhead. Lie on the floor of his tower library and look up, and the wooden beams of the ceiling are covered in sentences.
screen: `A NOTE ON THE MIRROR.` → `A CARD ON THE FRIDGE.` → `SENTENCES ON THE CEILING.`

segments.voice: First, the ceiling. Montaigne had short sayings painted along the beams and rafters of his library, in Latin and in Greek, the languages of the books on his shelves. So every time he looked up from his writing, there was a line waiting. Second, whose lines. The beams hold scripture and the classics side by side. Some come from scripture, from books like Ecclesiastes, with its long hard look at how little lasts. Some come from the old Roman and Greek writers. One borrowed from the Roman playwright Terence says, in Latin: I am a human being, and nothing human is foreign to me. Picture that one over your desk while you write about your own kidney stones and your own bad moods. It's almost permission. Third, why borrow at all. Montaigne's pages are full of other people's lines. In his essay on educating children, he gives his reason: he quotes others, he says, only to say himself better. The beams weren't decoration. They were company, voices he could argue with and lean on, sitting just above his head. Fourth, the beams at home. No ceiling or paintbrush needed. One sentence, put where the eye lands without hunting for it, does a slow kind of work. Read on a good day, it may get a nod. Read on a bad day, it can say something else. Given time, it can stop being words on a card and start being a voice in the room.
screen: `SAYINGS ON THE CEILING.` · `SCRIPTURE AND THE OLD WRITERS.` · `BORROWED TO SAY HIMSELF.` · `ONE LINE WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT.` · then, large: `ON THE BEAMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one saying where you'll see it. Sit for a moment and let the breath settle. Then let a line come to mind, one you already carry. Something from these months on the path, a verse, a poem, a thing your grandfather used to say, even a line of your own from a day here. Don't hunt for the best one; take the one that shows up. Hold it for a few breaths. Then, when the bell rings, write it somewhere your eyes will land: a mirror, a lock screen, the inside of a cupboard door. The bell holds the time.
Painted beams. The ceiling of Montaigne's library, lettered with sayings from scripture and the old writers, so a line was always waiting overhead. Today's word.
Your line: on the beams. Today, put one saying where you'll see it, and read it each time you pass, once on purpose. Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Some readers of Montaigne point to the painted beams of his library as a habit worth borrowing: keeping a few chosen sayings where the eye falls during an ordinary day.

notes: The Terence line and lines from Ecclesiastes are said to be among the beam inscriptions; the writer is fairly but not fully certain the Terence line is on the beams. Confirm against a published list of the inscriptions, or cut the example.
The Latin is quoted in the original-language game; Terence's word order varies by edition ('humani nihil a me' / 'humani a me nihil'). Confirm the form used on the beam.
'He quotes others only to say himself better' paraphrases Essays 1.26 ('Je ne dis les autres, sinon pour d'autant plus me dire'); confirm chapter numbering.
No count of inscriptions is given, deliberately.
